title: RBAC, Audit Logging, Data Residency, Secure SDLC, Incident Response, and Compliance Evidence Workflows
author: Asha Kapoor
body:
Summary and purpose

This document consolidates Redwood Inference’s operational controls and workflows across: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) and authentication, audit logging, data residency and retention, secure SDLC gates, incident response security procedures, compliance evidence collection, and risk & exceptions. It is intended for engineers, platform operators, product owners, compliance, and security reviewers.

Scope

Applies to: all production and staging environments, cloud accounts, internal admin consoles (Redwood Console), CI/CD pipelines that deploy production artifacts, and any customer-facing telemetry or audit pipelines. This includes Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments.

Owners and contacts

- Document owner: security (security-ops@redwood.com)
- Primary contacts: Asha Kapoor (Author), Daniel Reyes (Security Engineering), Maya Chen (Compliance)
- On-call escalation: security-oncall@redwood.com

1) RBAC and Authentication

Overview and principles
- Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP): Roles grant the minimal permissions required to perform tasks.
- Segregation of duties: Administrative tasks are separated across teams (infra, security, platform, product).
- Use centralized identity: SSO (OIDC/SAML) with corporate Identity Provider (IdP). No long-lived human credentials.
- Service accounts limited by scope and short-lived tokens when possible.

Defined roles and examples
- org-admin: full org-level configuration; reserved for senior operations / security.
- security-admin: audit, policy, incident response actions; can escalate to org-admin per emergency processes.
- infra-admin: ECS/K8s/GCP/AWS infra actions (provisioning, networking) but not billing or org-wide IAM.
- service-account (scoped): pipelines, autoscaling controllers, model-serving runtime; constrained by least-privilege policies.
- developer: read/write access to dev and staging; limited production access via time-bound tickets or just-in-time (JIT) roles.
- read-only: read-only dashboards and logs for non-admin staff.
- support: limited impersonation and troubleshooting privileges with full audit trail.

Authentication and MFA
- All human accounts must use SSO with MFA (TOTP + hardware key recommended).
- High-privilege roles require hardware-backed MFA (Security Key) enforced by IdP policy.
- Service-to-service authentication uses short-lived certificates or federated token exchange (no embedded long-lived secrets in repos).

Access granting, tenure, and reviews
- Access requests: via central Access Request Ticket (ART) system integrated with IdP for JIT elevation. Request must include justification, expiration, and approver.
- Onboarding: documented checklist that ensures least-privilege role assignment and training completion.
- Offboarding: automate deprovisioning on HR termination signals; revoke sessions and rotate impacted service tokens.
- Periodic review: quarterly access certification for all high-privilege roles; annual review for all other roles. Owners must attest.

RBAC policy example (conceptual)
- Example IAM-style policy (do not paste secrets):
  {
    \"version\": \"2022-01-01\",
    \"statements\": [
      {\"effect\": \"allow\", \"principal\": \"role:infra-admin\", \"actions\": [\"compute:manage-instances\", \"network:configure\"]}
    ]
  }

2) Audit logging

Logging objectives and coverage
- Purpose: provide reliable, tamper-evident records for forensic analysis, compliance audits (SOC2/ISO), and operational debugging.
- Events captured: authentication/login events, role/permission changes, privileged API calls, deployment actions, configuration changes, admin console activity, service account key lifecycle events, and data-export actions.

Retention and storage
- Production authentication & admin logs: retained 365 days by default.
- Security-critical audit logs (RBAC changes, incident traces): retained 3 years for SOC2/ISO evidence unless legal requires longer.
- Billing and financial evidence: retained 7 years to meet finance/legal obligations.
- Customer data access logs (per-customer residency preferences): retention configurable per-contract, default 365 days.

Integrity and protection
- All audit streams are written to an immutable, append-only store (WORM-capable object storage) and mirrored to a dedicated security analytics account.
- Logs are encrypted at rest (KMS-managed keys) and access-controlled by security-admin role.
- Archive signatures / manifests are generated and stored to detect tampering.

Alerting and SLOs
- Log delivery SLO: 99.9% of events ingested and indexed within 5 minutes for production services.
- Integrity check SLO: daily verification run; discrepancies investigated within 24 hours.

Example query and retention policy snippet (illustrative)
- Search for RBAC changes within 30 days:
  index=\"admin-audit\" source=\"rbac*\" | where action in (\"role.create\", \"role.update\", \"role.delete\") | sort by timestamp desc

3) Data residency and retention

Data residency model
- Redwood supports per-customer data residency controls in Hosted and Dedicated modes. Customers select region at onboarding (US, EU, APAC). Key control points: data at rest region, processing region, and log/event mirroring region.
- Private deployments follow customer-controlled infrastructure (customer-managed VPC); Redwood provides configuration guidance and verification checks.

Classification and retention schedule (default values)
- Authentication and audit logs: 365 days (security-critical subset archived 3 years).
- API request/response telemetry (customer content): default 30 days unless contract specifies otherwise; customers can opt-in to longer retention for debugging.
- Embeddings and model inputs stored for debugging: default 30 days; can be disabled or reduced to 0 days for regulated customers.
- Backups and snapshots: retained 90 days by default; encrypted and region-bound unless global backup required by customer.
- Billing & invoicing: 7 years.

Data deletion and export
- Customer data deletion requests: processed within 30 days for standard datasets; production snapshots may take up to 90 days to fully purge (documented to customer).
- Export: customers may request an encrypted data export (S3-compatible bundle) within 7 days of request; authentication and verification performed prior to export.

4) Secure SDLC (software development lifecycle)

Security gates and tooling
- Phase gates: Requirements -> Design & Threat Modeling -> Implementation (SCA & secret scanning) -> Pre-merge security checks -> Staging security smoke tests -> Release & Post-release monitoring.
- Mandatory tools: dependency SCA (software composition analysis), secret scanning, container image vulnerability scanning, SBOM generation on build, runtime policy checks (e.g., seccomp), and static analysis for critical services.

Threat modeling and design review
- All new services or significant changes (>= 2 engineers or external network access) require a short threat model document and a security design review. Template includes assets, trust boundaries, threat list, mitigations, and required controls.

Pre-release checklist (developer-facing)
1. Run SCA and resolve high/critical vulnerabilities or submit documented risk exception.
2. Ensure no secrets are in repo history.
3. Container image vulnerability scan: no critical CVEs.
4. SBOM attached to release artifact.
5. Unit + integration tests pass; security-focused tests executed.
6. Deployment manifests reviewed for least privilege and resource limits.
7. Rollback plan and runbook linked to release.

Penetration testing and third-party assessments
- Annual external penetration test for critical production services. Additional tests triggered by material architecture changes (e.g., new public endpoints).
- Vendor security questionnaires (VSA) and periodic reassessment for critical vendors.

5) Incident response security procedures

Goals and SLAs
- Goal: detect, contain, eradicate, recover, and learn with minimum customer impact.
- Initial triage SLA: 15 minutes for Sev1 (data exfiltration/service compromise), 1 hour for Sev2.
- Security lead must be engaged for any incident involving sensitive data, privileged access, or suspected exfiltration.

Incident phases and runbook summary
1. Detection & triage
   - Who: on-call SRE + security.
   - Actions: classify severity, notify stakeholders, and create incident channel.
2. Containment
   - Short-term containment: disable compromised credentials, revoke sessions, implement firewall or routing changes, isolate affected instances.
   - Preserve evidence: take snapshots of affected systems, preserve volatile logs.
3. Investigation & forensics
   - Do not run destructive remediation on live disks; capture forensic snapshots instead. Use dedicated forensic instances.
   - Collect audit logs, process lists, network captures, and container runtime metadata.
4. Remediation & recovery
   - Apply fixes, rotate secrets, redeploy known-good artifacts, and progressively restore services.
   - Validate integrity using checksums and audit comparisons.
5. Post-incident review
   - Draft RCA within 7 days for Sev1/Sev2; include timeline, impact, root cause, and action plan.

Evidence preservation commands (illustrative)
- Example AWS snapshot command:
  aws ec2 create-snapshot --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --description \"incident-2024-11-12-ec2-snapshot\"
- Example GCP:
  gcloud compute disks snapshot INSTANCE_DISK --snapshot-names=incident-2024-11-12-disk-snap --zone=ZONE
- Network capture (recommended to a separate forensic bucket):
  tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/incident-2024-11-12.pcap

Communications and compliance notifications
- Customer notification thresholds follow contractual SLAs. Security or Legal must approve external communication for incidents involving customer data.
- Regulatory notifications (e.g., GDPR data breach) executed per legal timelines after triage and assessment.

6) Compliance evidence collection workflows

Purpose
- Provide repeatable, auditable packages for external audits (SOC2/ISO27001), legal discovery, and internal attestations.

Automated evidence collector
- We maintain an automated evidence collector service that can assemble artifacts by evidence category and time window. Categories include access logs, configuration snapshots, change approvals, patch and deployment history, vulnerability scan reports, and policy documents.

Evidence package components (SOC2 example)
- Policies and procedures (signed and dated)
- Access control lists and user attestation records
- Change control tickets and deployment audit trails
- System and application logs for the audit period (integrity-verified)
- Pen test and vulnerability scan artifacts (with remediation evidence)
- Third-party vendor risk assessments and contracts
- Training and awareness records for staff

Packaging and signing
- Evidence packages are compiled into a time-stamped archive with a manifest. A member of Security signs the manifest and a copy is stored in the secure evidence vault.
- For high-sensitivity evidence, a notarized or legal-signed copy is available upon request.

Requesting evidence for audits
- Internal auditors or external assessors file an Evidence Request (ER) ticket indicating scope, time window, and required artifacts. Security/Compliance triage the ER within 3 business days and provide an ETA.

Retention and access
- Evidence packages for completed audits are retained for 7 years unless policy requires longer. Access to the evidence vault is role-restricted, logged, and requires an approved ER for retrieval.

7) Risk and exceptions process

Overview
- Some security controls may be infeasible short-term; a documented exception process allows controlled deviation with compensating controls and expiry.

Request process
1. Submit Risk Exception Request (RER) in the Risk system. Must include: scope, affected assets, justification, risk owner, compensating controls, proposed expiry, and mitigation plan.
2. Security reviews RER within 5 business days (expedited review for emergency exceptions).
3. If accepted, exception is recorded with approvals and assigned expiry. Quarterly re-attestation is required for active exceptions.

Approval criteria and compensating controls
- Exceptions are approved when residual risk is acceptable given compensating controls (e.g., enhanced monitoring, network segmentation, reduced blast radius, time-bound scope).
- The approver set includes security, the service owner, and compliance for high-impact requests.

Template fields (minimum)
- Title
- Service / asset(s) impacted
- Requested deviation and duration
- Business justification
- Risk owner and approver list
- Mitigations and monitoring plan
- Expiry date and re-evaluation cadence

Audit trail and enforcement
- All exceptions are logged in the Risk Register and surfaced to quarterly compliance reports. Exceptions older than expiry are automatically revoked unless re-approved.

Appendices

A. Quick-access checklists

Onboarding checklist for production access
- Request via ART with justification and approver
- Complete security training module
- Assigned role(s) validated by service owner
- MFA and SSO configured
- Access reviewed during quarterly certification

Incident response quick checklist (Sev1)
- Triage within 15 minutes and open incident channel
- Notify security-oncall and exec sponsor
- Preserve evidence (snapshots, logs) to secure bucket
- Rotate impacted credentials and revoke sessions
- Begin containment and follow runbook

B. Required artifacts for SOC2 evidence (short list)
- Access control policy and access reviews
- Change control evidence (PRD -> deployment ticket -> deploy artifact)
- Audit log exports for the scope period
- Vulnerability scans and remediation tickets

C. Related policies and runbooks
- security-and-compliance-playbook (master runbook)
- audit-logging-guidelines
- rbac-and-iam-standards (detailed IAM policies)
- secure-sdlc-checklist

D. Glossary and definitions
- PoLP: Principle of Least Privilege
- RBAC: Role-Based Access Control
- SCA: Software Composition Analysis
- SBOM: Software Bill of Materials
- RER: Risk Exception Request

Notes and next steps

- Action: Align default telemetry retention with new enterprise contracts and add per-customer retention SLAs to onboarding flow.

End of document
